newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian oil workers freed unharmed by guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian oil workers freed unharmed by guerrillas.

text.p: A group of Peruvian oil workers held in the jungle by Maoist Shining Path guerrillas were all released unharmed after rebels harangued them with political speeches and stole equipment, officials confirmed on Sunday.

"They are all out now. They are all out of the bush. It's over," an official at Peru's Compania General de Geofisica (CGG), who asked not to be identified, told Reuters in a telephone interview from the jungle town of Satipo.
He described the assailants as "a bunch of thieves," but refused to give more details about the incident.
Military and police sources had originally said that the approximately 30 oil workers involved were held between Friday and Sunday in the remote central jungle.
But some officials confirming their release said Shining Path only kept them for four hours on Friday.

"They did a proseltyzing work for four hours, giving ideological speeches to the workers," said police Capt. Mario Sanchez, from Satipo near the workers' camp. The rebels also stole food, fuel, medicines and communications equipment from the camp, he added.

An Interior Ministry spokesman in Lima, processing information from police and military sources, also said the incident had lasted four hours. He added that about 300 police and army soldiers were searching for the estimated 50- to 60-strong guerrilla patrol: "It seems we are getting close."

However, a journalist in the area, who asked not to be named, insisted he had evidence the hostages had been held until Sunday, and were transported to Satipo by helicopter after a deal had been struck with Shining Path involving the delivery of clothes and equipment.

Adding to the confusion, Satipo mayor Arturo Duran also said in a telephone interview the kidnapping lasted until Sunday, and added that the CGG had temporarily suspended operations, giving its workers leave until the end of the month.
CGG carries out exploration work in the dense and hilly River Ene region of central Peru for French oil company Elf. The CGG workers were all believed to be Peruvian.
Army foot patrols and at least two helicopters hunted for the rebels on Sunday, although military sources said they were probably in underground hideouts with traps nearby.

Shining Path and the MRTA have been highly active in the dense and isolated jungle area, mainly populated by Ashaninka indians, during a 17-year war on the state. Anti-terrorist police sources have said remnants of both groups -- severely reduced in recent years as a result of a government offensive - - were hiding in the zone.

The MRTA won world notoriety in December 1996 with the kidnapping of hundreds of guests at a Japanese embassy party. They held 72 of their highest-profile hostages for 126 days until Peru's military stormed the ambassador's residence, killing the 14 rebels and freeing all but one of the captives. Two soldiers and a hostage judge also died.

Overshadowed by the MRTA during the hostage crisis, Shining Path had been concentrating on regrouping forces and peasant education work, according to police. While the MRTA has been characterized by lucrative kidnappings, the Shining Path has generally raised money from involvement with drug-traffickers.
